issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
issues.explanation: 'Exposed to Others' is difficult to reconcile with toxic chemical exposure in this profile. It implies a visible, externally legible stigma or mark of trauma, but the rest of the profile does not include appearance-related injury, shame, or social-evaluative threat that would make this appraisal clinically coherent.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
issues.explanation: 'Inaction Guilt' is not impossible after a toxic exposure, but here it sits awkwardly with the rest of the formulation because no other item suggests a preventable omission, responsibility for others, or a scenario where the patient had a realistic chance to stop the event. In this profile it reads as insufficiently supported by the surrounding items.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
issues.explanation: 'Threat in Sounds' is a weak fit to the trauma type and to the rest of the selected items. Loud or unexpected sounds are not a natural trigger/threat cue for toxic chemical exposure unless the trauma involved explosions, alarms, or similarly salient auditory signals, which is not reflected elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
issues.explanation: For a 76-year-old male with trauma from toxic chemical exposure, the appraisal 'I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened' is the least coherent item in the profile. Toxic chemical exposure more plausibly yields themes of bodily damage, contamination, helplessness, or mistrust of the body/environment. Severe guilt about not preventing the event can occur, but here it is weakly supported by the rest of the profile: there are no memory, threat, trigger, or strategy items suggesting a role in causing the incident, failing to rescue others, or making a consequential decision. The other appraisal items are strongly body-focused and fit the trauma type well, making this guilt item stand out as insufficiently integrated with the formulation and surrounding content. The remaining items are clinically coherent with one another and with the active formulation pattern, especially the strong links among memory, threat, negative appraisals, and maladaptive strategies.

vignette:
Robert Hale was 76, a European American man living alone after a long divorce, and he had spent most of his working life managing a hotel in a busy Midwestern city. The event that now governed his days had taken place years earlier in the hotel’s basement maintenance corridor, when a storage area for cleaning supplies was mishandled and he was suddenly engulfed by a sharp chemical odor that stung his eyes, burned his throat, and made him feel as if his body had turned against him. He remembered stumbling toward the stairwell, unable to make sense of what he was breathing, with coworkers shouting somewhere above him and the corridor seeming to shrink around him. What stayed with Robert was not a tidy story but broken pieces: the sight of a mop bucket overturned on the concrete floor, the metallic taste in his mouth, the terrible smell that returned later in flashes, and, at other times, only the full wave of terror without any image at all. When he tried to think about it, the memory arrived in fragments that did not fit together, and sometimes the smell was so vivid he would grimace and cover his nose as if it were happening again.

In the months after the exposure, Robert began to treat his own body as unreliable, then as an enemy. He was certain that if his chest tightened or his stomach turned, it meant danger was already present, and he could not trust himself to tell the difference between memory and reality. That conviction made him constantly scan his body and his thoughts, waiting for the first sign that he was “going crazy” or that the chemical had done lasting damage. The more he noticed those sensations, the more convinced he became that he could not stop bad things from happening to him. He began feeling on guard even inside his own home, and certain places in the house—a chair by the window, the laundry room, the narrow hall near the basement door—felt like the only safe zones in a world that had become too large and too uncertain. Unexpected or loud sounds, especially a radiator clank or a car backfiring outside his apartment building, made him jump and stay tense for minutes afterward. His fear was not abstract; it was tied to the belief that his own body might betray him again without warning, and that the danger could appear anywhere.

Those sensations, and the half-formed memories behind them, also changed the way Robert handled his days. If a smell or a bodily flutter brought back that wash of terror, he would turn on the television or blast old music just to fill the room and keep his mind from settling on what he might feel next. He watched his thoughts closely, checking and rechecking them for signs that he was losing control, and if a fragment of the incident surfaced—a smell, a flash of the basement corridor, the scrape of work shoes on concrete—he would distract himself immediately rather than let it develop. At the hotel, where he still works part-time on familiar administrative tasks, he avoids the basement and the maintenance routes whenever he can, asking younger staff to handle anything that would take him near the old storage areas. He tells himself this is common sense, yet the relief is short-lived. The more he listens for every internal sensation and every unexpected sound, the more easily his body seems to react, and the more he becomes convinced that something is still wrong with him. In his view, the loud music and constant checking are attempts to stay in control, but they have also reinforced the sense that he is fragile and must monitor himself to keep disaster at bay.

By the time he came for help, Robert had become smaller in his own life. He had stopped meeting friends after work because restaurants and crowded lobbies felt too exposed, and he had begun arranging his errands around the few places that still felt tolerable. The memory still intruded in pieces, the smell still arrived when he least expected it, and every one of those moments tightened his sense that danger was near and his body could not be trusted. What finally brought him in was his worry that the circle had become unlivable: he was spending more time guarding against signs of catastrophe than actually living, and he feared that if he did not get help he would remain trapped in a world that felt unsafe everywhere except in a handful of rooms. He wanted, more than anything, to trust his body again and to stop feeling as though disaster was always about to begin.
